feed.subtitle: Short dispatches from the intersection of mud, models and megawatts

entry.title: Every prompt has a footprint — so what?
entry.summary: A watt-hour means nothing to most people.
entry.content:
A watt-hour means nothing to most people. The same answer counted in phone charges or cups of coffee does. At the Digital Society School I helped build decision tools for a Dutch government partner around exactly that translation — because the gap between the most and least efficient model on the same task can exceed an order of magnitude, and few tools put that in front of the person typing the prompt.

The point is not AI guilt. It's the same soft-path thinking I learned in water management: before you build a bigger pipe — or call a bigger model — ask whether the demand itself can be smarter. Try the EcoPrompt Coach chart on the homepage; that's the argument, running live.

Corrected October 2026: this first said "I'm building"; that work ended in February 2026.

entry.title: Why I wrote a pessimistic future on purpose
entry.summary: Model output alone seldom moves a decision; a story people can picture often does.
entry.content:
My Wageningen thesis ended with "Dirty Delta" — a deliberately dark storyline for Africa's coastal waters by mid-century. Model output alone seldom moves a decision; a story people can picture often does. Turning regression coefficients on income, urbanisation and agriculture into a narrative was the most useful translation work I've done.

The lesson survived the thesis: if your analysis can't be retold in a corridor after the meeting, it rarely counts. I now write the storyline first and let it set the questions for the numbers, never the answers.

Wording softened in October 2026.

entry.title: What 164 water points taught me about data
entry.summary: Geophysics taught me that data only matters when someone stakes something on it.
entry.content:
In hard rock, a wrong guess isn't a bad cell in a spreadsheet — it's a dry hole a community paid for. Geophysics taught me that data only matters when someone stakes something on it. The boreholes we sited from resistivity surveys struck water 70% of the time, and every strike was the same lesson: collect the data before the drill bit, not after.

I carry that into every analysis I do now. The question is never "what does the data say?" — it's "who is about to spend money, or drink water, based on what I claim it says?"

Corrected October 2026: the 70% is a share of the holes drilled, not a gain over drilling blind.
